title: Stable Continuous-Time Consistency Distillation:An Empirical Study with a Multistep Extension

paper.title:
Stable Continuous-Time Consistency Distillation: An Empirical Study with a Multistep Extension Thanks: Part of the work was done while William KM Lai was at Cornell University.
Correspondence to: wklai2@buffalo.edu
paper.abstract: Abstract Continuous-time consistency models are an attractive route to few-step generation. They remove the discretization error inherent to the timestep grid that discrete-time consistency models depend on. Until recently, however, training them was unstable. Lu and Song (2025) address this with the TrigFlow formulation and a coordinated set of architectural and training-objective changes. We conduct an independent empirical study of this framework on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64. No open-weight TrigFlow teachers exist at these scales, so we train them from scratch and then verify the consistency distillation (sCD) and consistency training (sCT) behavior of students initialized from these teachers. On CIFAR-10, our students reproduce the reported FID at one and two steps. On ImageNet-64, they fall short, a gap that appears related to our teacher and to architectural choices the paper leaves unspecified. We also report a parameter-count gap of about 5 % 5\% between the model size stated in the paper and a faithful re-implementation, which we attribute to the scale-and-shift conditioning projections in Adaptive Double Normalization. We then propose Multistep sCD (MS-sCD) , a continuous-time, segment-conditioned multistep generalization of sCD. The segment-conditioning idea is borrowed from the discrete-time multistep consistency distillation of Heek et al. (2024) ; we build on their preliminary continuous-time experiments within the TrigFlow/sCM framework. The rest of the algorithm follows sCD. MS-sCD replaces sCM’s two-step intermediate time with a fixed segment-boundary schedule and recovers sCD at M = 1 M=1 . We report FID at M = 2 , 4 , 8 M=2,4,8 and compare against the discrete-time MSCD baseline. Code, model weights, and training scripts are available on GitHub ( Mathew et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: 1.1 Motivation
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ; Karras et al., 2022 ) produce high-quality samples but require many sequential network evaluations. Distillation reduces this cost by training a student to generate samples in fewer steps, but methods differ in what they ask the student to learn. Progressive distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) repeatedly halves the sampling steps by teaching each student to match two steps of the previous model. Consistency models ( Song et al., 2023 ) instead learn to map points on the same probability-flow ODE trajectory to a common endpoint, enabling one- or few-step generation with a single network. Later methods ( Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) refine the loss, timestep sampling, and weighting, while multistep consistency distillation (MSCD) ( Heek et al., 2024 ) divides the trajectory into segments so that each prediction covers a shorter interval. MSCD uses DDIM ( Song et al., 2021a ) teacher steps within these segments and an aDDIM sampler to correct the variance shortfall of finite DDIM integration. A separate direction compares distributions rather than enforcing consistency along trajectories: variational score distillation ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , distribution matching distillation ( Yin et al., 2024 ) , and moment matching ( Salimans et al., 2024 ) use distribution-level objectives. For consistency models, a remaining question is whether training can avoid the timestep grid and its discretization error. Song et al. (2023) propose a continuous-time formulation (their Appendix B), but report training instability. The main iCT results of Song and Dhariwal (2024) use discrete-time training. sCM ( Lu and Song, 2025 ) addresses this instability through the TrigFlow parameterization and coordinated changes to time conditioning, normalization, and the training objective, reporting stable continuous-time CMs at scales up to 1.5B parameters on ImageNet-512. We examine whether these results can be reproduced and whether segment-conditioned distillation extends the framework to larger sampling budgets.

sections.heading: 1.2 Contributions
sections.text: Our contributions are: 1. Reproduction with implementation clarifications. We reproduce sCM’s TrigFlow teacher and sCD/sCT students on CIFAR-10 (unconditional, DDPM++ backbone) and ImageNet-64 (class-conditional, EDM2-S backbone), following the two configurations sCM uses. We make explicit the implementation details required to run the continuous-time CM training loop. 2. Continuous-time MS-sCD (extension). Building on Heek et al. (2024) ’s preliminary experiments with segment-conditioned continuous-time training, we derive, implement, and evaluate this approach within the TrigFlow/sCM framework. 3. Comparisons with existing methods. We compare MS-sCD with MSCD ( Heek et al., 2024 ) on the same EDM2-S backbone to assess their relative strengths at different sampling budgets. We also evaluate moment matching ( Salimans et al., 2024 ) on an ADM-style backbone to examine an alternative distillation objective.

sections.heading: 2.6 Multistep Consistency Distillation
sections.text: Heek et al. (2024) discretize the generation trajectory into M M segments with boundaries 0 = t 0 < t 1 < ⋯ < t M 0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{M} , train a shared network across segments, and use DDIM teacher steps within each segment. They propose the aDDIM correction to compensate for the variance shortfall of finite DDIM steps. The paper trains on the discrete grid. It also notes that continuous-time training is possible provided the model takes an extra conditioning signal that identifies the current segment (so the prediction can change discontinuously across segment boundaries), and reports that early experiments with this variant worked comparably ( Heek et al., 2024 , §3). Our MS-sCD (Section 6 ) builds on this approach by adding a segment-boundary input t k t_{k} to the network and training in continuous time within the TrigFlow CM framework.

sections.heading: 3.1 Backbones
sections.text: We train at two settings, matching sCM’s own backbone choices. CIFAR-10 ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) (unconditional, 32 × 32 32{\times}32 ) uses the Score SDE DDPM++ network of Song et al. (2021b) with the EDM 2022 ( Karras et al., 2022 ) training settings. ImageNet-64 (class-conditional, 64 × 64 64{\times}64 ) is a downsampled version of ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ; Russakovsky et al., 2015 ) and uses the magnitude-preserving EDM2 UNet ( Karras et al., 2024 ) . Both carry the TrigFlow parameterization, identity time conditioning, positional time embeddings, and ADN (Section 2.5 ). The EDM2 backbone is built from magnitude-preserving convolutions and uses EDM2’s normalize ( ε = 10 − 4 \varepsilon=10^{-4} ) for the pixel normalization inside ADN. DDPM++ has no weight-normalized layers and instead applies the PGGAN pixel norm ( Karras et al., 2018 ) ( ε = 10 − 8 \varepsilon=10^{-8} ) that sCM cites. The rest of the section covers implementation choices that the paper leaves unspecified.

sections.heading: 3.2 ADN block and parameter count
sections.text: ADN modulates every residual block as y ⋅ pnorm ⁡ ( s ) + pnorm ⁡ ( b ) y\cdot\mathrm{pnorm}(s)+\mathrm{pnorm}(b) , with the scale s s and shift b b produced by a single linear projection of the time embedding. The same offset is expected at the larger model sizes.

sections.heading: 4.3 sCD vs. sCT
sections.text: The two variants share the loss in equation 11 and differ only in where the tangent d ​ x t / d ​ t dx_{t}/dt comes from, which we gave in Section 4.1 . sCD requires two forward passes per training step, while sCT requires one. We initialize the student from the teacher’s weights in both cases. This is easy to overlook for sCT, which is usually described as teacher-free. Algorithm 1 of Lu and Song (2025) sets θ ← θ pretrain \theta\leftarrow\theta_{\text{pretrain}} , and the appendix says so directly, so the weights themselves still come from the diffusion teacher. That is the real difference from the train-from-scratch consistency training of Song et al. (2023) .

sections.heading: 6.1 Motivation
sections.text: sCM’s two-step sampling uses a fixed intermediate time t mid = 1.1 t_{\text{mid}}=1.1 , whose optimal value varies with model size and training duration. More broadly, sCM’s multi-step generation applies a single-step CM repeatedly, whereas MSCD trains a shared network across segments and runs one step per segment (Figure 1 ). The sCM authors list “incorporating our proposed techniques into multi-step consistency models” as future work, and Heek et al. (2024) note that continuous-time training of an MSCD-style model is possible if the network takes an explicit conditioning signal identifying the current segment, so that the prediction can change discontinuously across segment boundaries. MS-sCD combines these two ideas. We add a segment-boundary input t k t_{k} to the sCM network through a zero-initialized embedding, so the model reduces to sCM at M = 1 M=1 and becomes a segment-conditioned multistep CM otherwise. Three things change as a result: the segment CM parameterization (Section 6.2 ), its JVP target (Section 6.3 ), and the training procedure (Section 6.4 ).

sections.heading: 7 Supporting Context: MSCD and Moment Matching
sections.text: Before training the TrigFlow models we reproduced two existing distillation methods on class-conditional ImageNet-64, using the EDM framework ( Karras et al., 2022 ) with the ADM-style UNet of Dhariwal and Nichol (2021) , to validate our 50k-sample FID pipeline against published numbers. Our Multistep Consistency Distillation (MSCD, Heek et al. 2024 ) student reaches FID ≈ 2.3 {\approx}2.3 at 8 steps, matching the deterministic Heun teacher at 511 NFE. This is the same method we later port to the EDM2-S backbone as the discrete-time baseline for MS-sCD (Table 4 ). Because MSCD trains the student to follow the deterministic teacher ODE within each segment, it is expected that the teacher quality has an influence on its FID. We separately reproduced moment matching ( Salimans et al., 2024 ) , a distribution-matching distillation, on the same backbone, reaching FID ≈ 1.4 {\approx}1.4 with an 8-step student. We do not pursue this family further. The contrast is worth noting all the same. On images, distribution-matching distillation reaches much lower few-step FID than the trajectory-matching consistency objectives we focus on.

sections.heading: 8.1 The teacher gap propagates to the distilled students
sections.text: Our TrigFlow teacher reaches FID 1.83 1.83 on ImageNet-64 against the reported 1.70 1.70 (Table 1 ). Since sCD distills the teacher ODE, teacher quality may contribute to our sCD-S shortfall. The sCT-S gap, which does not distill the teacher, must have a separate cause (Section 8.2 ). The teacher deficit also reframes the multistep route: a one-step student must absorb the entire teacher-to-data map in a single evaluation, whereas MSCD and MS-sCD divide it across M M segments and lower the per-step burden, tracking the teacher more closely at the same total compute. We therefore expect that, with the residual teacher gap closed, the multistep budget–quality trade-off is the more dependable use of a fixed sampling budget at small model scale.

sections.heading: 8.2 sCT vs. sCD ordering depends on model capacity
sections.text: Lu and Song (2025) state in their Discussions and Limitations section that “sCT consistently outperforms sCD on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 64 × 64 64{\times}64 but is less effective than sCD across different model scales on ImageNet 512 × 512 512{\times}512 ,” attributing the ImageNet- 512 512 exception to the training variance of CT in latent spaces with imperfect encoders. The same paper’s appendix table at ImageNet- 64 64 (sCM Table 8) reports sCT-S at FID 3.23 3.23 / 2.93 2.93 (1-/2-step) versus sCD-S at 2.97 2.97 / 2.07 2.07 , so sCT is worse than sCD at the smallest model size by ≈ 0.26 {\approx}0.26 at NFE = 1 {=}1 and ≈ 0.86 {\approx}0.86 at NFE = 2 {=}2 . From size M upward the ordering reverses (sCT-M 2.25 2.25 / 1.81 1.81 vs. sCD-M 2.79 2.79 / 1.89 1.89 ), and sCT wins through XL as the paper’s claim suggests. The blanket statement therefore holds only at the larger scales. At EDM2-S the ordering is reversed even in a pixel-space setting where the latent-space hypothesis does not apply. The sCT/sCD ordering is therefore capacity-dependent, not purely dataset-dependent.

sections.heading: 8.3 Backbone-dependent reproduction quality on CIFAR-10 versus ImageNet-64
sections.text: On CIFAR-10 our sCD matches and slightly exceeds the reported FID at both step counts. On ImageNet-64, sCD-S lags by ≈ 0.6 {\approx}0.6 FID and sCT-S by more. These results do not establish the cause of the gap. Two implementation choices specific to ImageNet-64 may contribute, but we have not tested them in controlled ablations. Adaptive-weighting head w ϕ ​ ( t ) w_{\phi}(t) . sCM specifies the weighting objective but not the architecture of w ϕ w_{\phi} , only that it follows EDM2 (a Fourier embedding into a magnitude-preserving linear map). We use a positional embedding of t t instead, matching sCM’s documented Fourier-to-positional substitution for the main network, which the paper does not extend explicitly to the weighting head. Attention implementation. sCM states that the ImageNet-64 students use FlashAttention with a custom JVP rule, but the released EDM2 backbone uses an einsum attention by default (its notes flag the fused kernel as insufficiently tested). We follow that default. The FlashAttention path and its JVP rule cannot be reconstructed from the available artifacts, and the FP16 reduction-order difference could accumulate over the 400 400 k-iteration student schedule. Two architectural details are unspecified, and other undocumented implementation choices may also contribute to the gap.

sections.heading: 9 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: We set out to reproduce the TrigFlow/sCM formulation and to see how far it extends. The three architectural changes address the terms in equation 6 , while the three objective changes modify the training gradient. On CIFAR-10, we recover the reported sCD FID at both step counts. On ImageNet-64, our teacher does not reach the reported 1.70 1.70 , and the students also fall short. Implementation differences may contribute to these gaps, but we have not isolated their effects. Our MS-sCD results show that segment-conditioned distillation can be trained within the continuous-time sCD framework. FID improves as the number of segments increases on both datasets. On ImageNet-64, MS-sCD outperforms iterative sCD sampling at the same NFE, while its advantage over discrete-time MSCD is limited to the smaller step budgets. These findings are limited to pixel-space generation at 32 × 32 32{\times}32 and 64 × 64 64{\times}64 resolution. Evaluating the method at higher resolutions, in latent spaces, and for text-to-image generation is left to future work.

sections.heading: Appendix B Dropout in Multistep Consistency Models
sections.text: Discrete MSCD uses two student forward passes per step. We synchronize their dropout masks by saving and restoring the random state, following Song and Dhariwal (2024) . This prevents dropout randomness from contributing to the consistency residual. In our MSCD reproductions on EDM ( Karras et al., 2022 ) and EDM2 ( Karras et al., 2024 ) , students without dropout overfit within the training budget. Our single-step sCD runs use zero dropout, following Lu and Song (2025, Appendix G.2) . Continuous MS-sCD computes the prediction and its time derivative in one JVP forward pass, so they share a dropout mask without explicit synchronization. For MS-sCD, no dropout led to overfitting and an eight-step FID near 2.3 2.3 ; a rate of 0.2 0.2 slowed training and showed signs of instability. We use 0.1 0.1 at resolutions ≤ 16 \leq 16 for all reported MS-sCD results.

sections.heading: Appendix C Noise Sampling for the Multistep Students
sections.text: Heek et al. (2024) split diffusion time into equal segments and sample the training noise uniformly over a discrete, cosine-parameterized step grid that anneals from 64 64 to 1280 1280 steps. We instead use framework-specific noise schedules. For the discrete MSCD on EDM2-S we use the teacher’s EDM (Karras) σ \sigma grid, annealing the step count from 64 64 to 1280 1280 . For MS-sCD we keep the segment boundaries uniform in TrigFlow time but sample σ \sigma from a log-normal proposal ( P mean = − 1.0 P_{\text{mean}}=-1.0 , P std = 1.6 P_{\text{std}}=1.6 ; teacher: P mean = − 0.8 P_{\text{mean}}=-0.8 ) and set t = arctan ⁡ ( σ / σ d ) t=\arctan(\sigma/\sigma_{d}) , instead of spreading samples evenly across segments. This global proposal worked better in our runs. Spreading samples evenly across segments puts too much weight on noise levels the teacher rarely saw in training. For the two-step ( M = 2 M{=}2 ) discrete MSCD on EDM2 we set the intermediate segment boundary of the student grid to σ = 1.1 \sigma=1.1 , giving [ σ max , 1.1 , 0 ] [\sigma_{\max},1.1,0] , since the default Karras schedule places it near σ min = 0.002 \sigma_{\min}=0.002 and collapses the first segment. The M = 4 M{=}4 runs keep the default Karras grid.

sections.text: Table 5 extends MS-sCD to unconditional CIFAR-10. Increasing M M improves FID, but M = 8 M{=}8 ( 2.20 2.20 ) does not surpass our two-step sCT ( 2.09 2.09 ). A useful reference point is the teacher ODE itself: the same TrigFlow checkpoint that reaches FID 2.08 2.08 at the standard 35-NFE DPM-Solver-2S setting ( Lu and Song, 2025 ; Karras et al., 2022 ) evaluates to FID 2.22 2.22 at 199 NFE. For an exact PF-ODE, more steps should reduce numerical integration error ( Karras et al., 2022 ; Lu et al., 2022 ) ; FID, however, measures samples from the learned vector field, so its dependence on NFE need not be monotone when model error or solver/schedule mismatch dominates. They remove the discretization error inherent to the timestep grid that discrete-time consistency models depend on. Until recently, however, training them was unstable. Lu and Song (2025) address this with the TrigFlow formulation and a coordinated set of architectural and training-objective changes. We conduct an independent empirical study of this framework on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64. No open-weight TrigFlow teachers exist at these scales, so we train them from scratch and then verify the consistency distillation (sCD) and consistency training (sCT) behavior of students initialized from these teachers. On CIFAR-10, our students reproduce the reported FID at one and two steps. On ImageNet-64, they fall short, a gap that appears related to our teacher and to architectural choices the paper leaves unspecified. We also report a parameter-count gap of about 5 % 5\% between the model size stated in the paper and a faithful re-implementation, which we attribute to the scale-and-shift conditioning projections in Adaptive Double Normalization. We then propose Multistep sCD (MS-sCD) , a continuous-time, segment-conditioned multistep generalization of sCD. The segment-conditioning idea is borrowed from the discrete-time multistep consistency distillation of Heek et al. (2024) ; we build on their preliminary continuous-time experiments within the TrigFlow/sCM framework. The rest of the algorithm follows sCD. MS-sCD replaces sCM’s two-step intermediate time with a fixed segment-boundary schedule and recovers sCD at M = 1 M=1 . We report FID at M = 2 , 4 , 8 M=2,4,8 and compare against the discrete-time MSCD baseline. Code, model weights, and training scripts are available on GitHub ( Mathew et al., 2026 ) . Reviewed on OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=di6ofoWEU8 1 Introduction 1.1 Motivation Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ; Karras et al., 2022 ) produce high-quality samples but require many sequential network evaluations. Distillation reduces this cost by training a student to generate samples in fewer steps, but methods differ in what they ask the student to learn. Progressive distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) repeatedly halves the sampling steps by teaching each student to match two steps of the previous model. Consistency models ( Song et al., 2023 ) instead learn to map points on the same probability-flow ODE trajectory to a common endpoint, enabling one- or few-step generation with a single network. Later methods ( Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ; Geng et al., 2025 ) refine the loss, timestep sampling, and weighting, while multistep consistency distillation (MSCD) ( Heek et al., 2024 ) divides the trajectory into segments so that each prediction covers a shorter interval. MSCD uses DDIM ( Song et al., 2021a ) teacher steps within these segments and an aDDIM sampler to correct the variance shortfall of finite DDIM integration. A separate direction compares distributions rather than enforcing consistency along trajectories: variational score distillation ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , distribution matching distillation ( Yin et al., 2024 ) , and moment matching ( Salimans et al., 2024 ) use distribution-level objectives. For consistency models, a remaining question is whether training can avoid the timestep grid and its discretization error. Song et al. (2023) propose a continuous-time formulation (their Appendix B), but report training instability. The main iCT results of Song and Dhariwal (2024) use discrete-time training. sCM ( Lu and Song, 2025 ) addresses this instability through the TrigFlow parameterization and coordinated changes to time conditioning, normalization, and the training objective, reporting stable continuous-time CMs at scales up to 1.5B parameters on ImageNet-512. We examine whether these results can be reproduced and whether segment-conditioned distillation extends the framework to larger sampling budgets. 1.2 Contributions Our contributions are: 1. Reproduction with implementation clarifications. We reproduce sCM’s TrigFlow teacher and sCD/sCT students on CIFAR-10 (unconditional, DDPM++ backbone) and ImageNet-64 (class-conditional, EDM2-S backbone), following the two configurations sCM uses. We make explicit the implementation details required to run the continuous-time CM training loop. 2. Continuous-time MS-sCD (extension). Building on Heek et al. Our Multistep Consistency Distillation (MSCD, Heek et al. 2024 ) student reaches FID ≈ 2.3 {\approx}2.3 at 8 steps, matching the deterministic Heun teacher at 511 NFE. This is the same method we later port to the EDM2-S backbone as the discrete-time baseline for MS-sCD (Table 4 ). Because MSCD trains the student to follow the deterministic teacher ODE within each segment, it is expected that the teacher quality has an influence on its FID. We separately reproduced moment matching ( Salimans et al., 2024 ) , a distribution-matching distillation, on the same backbone, reaching FID ≈ 1.4 {\approx}1.4 with an 8-step student. We do not pursue this family further. The contrast is worth noting all the same. On images, distribution-matching distillation reaches much lower few-step FID than the trajectory-matching consistency objectives we focus on. 8 Discussion 8.1 The teacher gap propagates to the distilled students Our TrigFlow teacher reaches FID 1.83 1.83 on ImageNet-64 against the reported 1.70 1.70 (Table 1 ). Since sCD distills the teacher ODE, teacher quality may contribute to our sCD-S shortfall. The sCT-S gap, which does not distill the teacher, must have a separate cause (Section 8.2 ). The teacher deficit also reframes the multistep route: a one-step student must absorb the entire teacher-to-data map in a single evaluation, whereas MSCD and MS-sCD divide it across M M segments and lower the per-step burden, tracking the teacher more closely at the same total compute. We therefore expect that, with the residual teacher gap closed, the multistep budget–quality trade-off is the more dependable use of a fixed sampling budget at small model scale. 8.2 sCT vs. sCD ordering depends on model capacity Lu and Song (2025) state in their Discussions and Limitations section that “sCT consistently outperforms sCD on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 64 × 64 64{	imes}64 but is less effective than sCD across different model scales on ImageNet 512 × 512 512{	imes}512 ,” attributing the ImageNet- 512 512 exception to the training variance of CT in latent spaces with imperfect encoders.
